content: Delavirdine has not been included in the recommended regimens for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), as a class of antiretroviral agents, are known for their rapid action and high potency, which makes them conceptually appealing for PEP. Additionally, there is some evidence supporting their prophylactic efficacy. However, concerns regarding side effects and the availability of alternative agents argue against the routine use of NNRTIs for initial PEP regimens. Nevertheless, with expert consultation, the use of an NNRTI may be considered in specific cases. An essential goal of PEP is to promote and facilitate adherence to the 4-week PEP regimen. Therefore, the toxicity profile of antiretroviral agents, including the frequency, severity, duration, and reversibility of side effects, is a critical consideration. All antiretroviral agents have been associated with side effects. However, most studies on adverse events have been conducted in individuals with advanced disease undergoing longer treatment courses, which may not accurately reflect the experiences of individuals with less advanced disease or those who are uninfected. The incidence of adverse effects, such as nausea or diarrhea, has generally not been higher when these agents are used in combination. All approved protease inhibitors (PIs) have the potential for serious drug interactions when used with certain other medications. This necessitates careful evaluation of concomitant medications being taken by healthcare workers (HCWs) before prescribing a PI and close monitoring for toxicity during treatment. PIs may inhibit the metabolism of non-sedating antihistamines and other drugs metabolized by the liver. Additionally, nelfinavir (NEL) and ritonavir may accelerate the clearance of certain drugs, including oral contraceptives, requiring alternative or additional contraceptive measures for women taking these medications. The use of PIs has also been associated with the onset of diabetes mellitus, hyperglycemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, and exacerbation of pre-existing diabetes mellitus. Rare cases of hemolytic anemia have been linked to the use of indinavir (IDV). Nelfinavir, saquinavir, and ritonavir have been associated with the development of diarrhea, although this side effect typically responds to treatment with antimotility agents, which can be prescribed at the time these drugs are initiated for PEP. The manufacturer's package insert should always be consulted for questions regarding potential drug interactions. In studies where higher-than-recommended doses of certain antiretroviral agents were used, 50% to 75% of individuals reported one or more subjective complaints, and approximately 30% discontinued the drug due to symptoms. Commonly reported symptoms included nausea, vomiting, malaise or fatigue, headache, and insomnia. Mild decreases in hemoglobin levels and absolute neutrophil counts were also observed.
